title: The complete marketplace — what things are

steps.path: Everything you can get from it
steps.headline: Everything in the marketplace is one of three things: a listing, a part, or a collection.
steps.changed: A listing is one thing an author publishes: you install, update, remove, rate, comment on and report a listing, and it carries one safety result. A part is one usable piece inside it (a skill, a command, a specialist, a tool connection, a page, a theme). A collection is a named list of listings.
steps.notice: A skill still gets its own card with 'Part of Superpowers', as you decided in April. But its card never has its own rating or its own Install: it says 'Get Superpowers'. Ratings stop being split between a plugin and the pieces inside it.

steps.path: A plugin with many pieces inside
steps.headline: When you want just one piece of a big plugin, what should happen?
steps.today: Wanting one skill out of a plugin with 23 installs all 23, and all 23 show up in your skills list. There is no way to switch any of them off.
steps.problem: Your list fills with things you never asked for. Installing one piece alone was put off in August and never built.
steps.proposal: Pick how one piece is handled.

options.label: Install it all, switch pieces on
options.summary: The whole plugin arrives; you tick which pieces you want to see and use.
pros: Your lists show only what you chose.
What is on your computer always matches a version we checked, so the safety result stays true.
Turning another piece on later is instant, with no download.
cons: The unused pieces still take a little disk space.

options.label: Download only that piece
pros: Nothing extra on your computer.
cons: Pieces often rely on each other, so a lone one can quietly not work.
A half-plugin matches no version we checked, so its safety result means less.
Updates get complicated: which half are you on?

steps.headline: Every kind of thing lives in one marketplace with one set of rules, including Pages.
steps.changed: Today plugins, themes and sign-in connections are three separate lists built three different ways, and Pages were headed for a fourth. They become one. A Page, a theme, a specialist or a prompt is a listing like any other: it has a version, an author, a safety result, votes, comments and updates.
steps.notice: Themes get comments and 'what changed'. Pages get everything plugins have. One search covers all of it. The Themes view and the Connections row stay; they become filters over the same list.

steps.intro: Your words from 6 October: 'I want it all to basically work like GitHub for norms.' These turn that into plain actions.

steps.headline: Anything you install can be made yours, and every change can be undone.
steps.changed: Any installed thing (a Page, a theme, a plugin, a specialist, a prompt) can be changed by hand or by asking the assistant. It is then marked 'Your version' and remembers what it came from. A History list shows every change, yours and the author's, and restores any earlier point.
steps.notice: A 'Make it mine' action on installed things, a 'Your version' tag, and a History menu like the one in a document editor. No git words anywhere.

steps.path: When the original gets an update
steps.headline: When the original changes, you are told, and the assistant can carry your changes onto the new version.
steps.changed: From your 24 October note: be 'informed of changes/updates to the original' and 'rebase your page agentically'. The update offers three choices: Update and keep my changes (the assistant blends them, shows you a preview, and it can be undone), Replace with the new one, or Keep mine.
steps.notice: One extra choice on updates to things you changed. Blending will sometimes fail on big changes; it then says so and leaves you the other two choices. Your old copy is always in History.

steps.path: Many versions of the same thing
steps.headline: When ten people publish their own version of a Page, how should they appear?
steps.today: Nothing links one listing to another. Ten versions would be ten unrelated cards.
steps.problem: You said: 'show on one page like all given pages that are like a variant of it. Or like the parent pages.' Ten near-identical cards would also crowd browsing.
steps.proposal: Every listing page gets a Family section: what it is based on, and versions made by others. Pick how versions show while browsing.

options.label: Grouped under the original
options.summary: One card that says '10 versions'. A version that becomes more popular than the original gets its own card.
pros: Browsing stays clean.
The original author keeps the credit and the traffic.
A better version still rises on its own merit.
cons: A good version is one tap deeper until it earns its own card.

options.label: Every version is its own card
pros: Each version is seen straight away.
cons: Lists fill with near-duplicates.
Copy-and-rename becomes a way to grab attention.

steps.headline: Should you be able to send your improvement back to the original author?
steps.today: Improving someone's plugin means knowing GitHub. Ordinary users cannot do it.
steps.problem: You said the point is to 'make that free shit better' together. Without a way back, every improvement stays stuck in one person's copy, or becomes yet another version.
steps.proposal: Yes: a 'Suggest to the author' action. The author sees a plain summary of what changed, can try it, and accepts or declines; accepted work is credited to you. No: improvements travel only as separate published versions.

steps.path: Telling the author something is broken
steps.headline: Every listing gets 'Report a problem', which goes to its author, separate from reporting it as unsafe.
steps.changed: You said: 'I want people to be able to report bugs for pages and marketplace plugins.' A problem report goes to the author and is counted on the listing ('3 open problems'). A safety report goes to us and can lead to the listing being turned off.
steps.notice: Two clearly different buttons. Listings with many unanswered problems rank lower.

steps.headline: How should a person with no GitHub account publish what they made?
steps.today: Publishing needs a GitHub account. On 24 October you kept that 'for now' and asked for the costs and risks of anything else before deciding.
steps.problem: The people this is for are the ones without GitHub accounts. Requiring one shuts them out of sharing.
steps.proposal: Everything is still stored on GitHub underneath. Pick who holds it.

options.label: YouCoded submits it for them
options.summary: They press Publish while signed in to YouCoded. We store it in a GitHub space we own.
pros: Anyone can publish in one press.
Storage costs nothing.
Nothing goes public until it passes the checks.
cons: We become the named host: complaints and takedown requests come to us.
Junk and spam need limits per account and someone watching the queue.

options.label: Keep requiring GitHub
pros: No hosting duty for us.
cons: Most everyday users never publish.

options.label: Our own storage
pros: Full control, no reliance on GitHub.
cons: A monthly bill that grows with every published thing.
Backups, abuse and outages become ours.
Hard to justify while GitHub is free.

steps.path: The name for making your own copy
steps.headline: What should the app call making your own changeable copy of something?
steps.today: Programmers call it a fork. The app has no word for it yet.
steps.problem: The word appears on a button, a tag and the family list, so it has to be obvious to someone who has never heard of GitHub.

options.label: Make it mine / Your version
pros: Says what happens with no explanation.
cons: Two phrases rather than one word.

options.label: Remix
pros: One friendly word, familiar from music and video apps.
cons: Sounds playful for something like a budget Page.

options.label: Fork
pros: The word programmers already use.
cons: Means nothing to everyone else.

steps.intro: The live marketplace holds about 4,000 listings, shown in alphabetical order. These decide how the good ones are found.

steps.path: Filtering by what something is for
steps.headline: How should listings be sorted into topics?
steps.today: There are three topic systems. One is never shown. One is filled in on 9 listings. The 'Vibe' menu covers 10 listings, so picking a vibe shows almost nothing.
steps.problem: With 4,000 listings nobody can tag them by hand, so the filters are empty and browsing by interest does not work.
steps.proposal: One list of about twelve plain topics (Writing, School, Work, Money, Home, Health, Fun, Research, Design, Coding, Data, Automation). Pick who fills it in.

options.label: AI sorts, you can correct
pros: Every listing has a topic from day one, including new ones.
A wrong one is fixed by hand and stays fixed.
cons: Some will be sorted wrongly until someone notices.
A small running cost each time a listing changes.

options.label: Authors choose
pros: The person who knows the plugin best decides.
cons: Most listings are imported from outside lists whose authors will never choose, so most stay empty.

steps.path: What you see when it opens
steps.headline: Most listings are tools for programmers. What should a new person see first?
steps.today: Everything is mixed together. Most of the 4,000 are developer tools imported from other lists; the everyday ones (journaling, Google, Spotify, themes) are a small share.
steps.problem: The app is for students and everyday users as much as programmers. A wall of database and deployment tools tells them it is not for them.
steps.proposal: Each listing is marked Everyday or Coding. Pick how the split is used.

options.label: Everyday first, Coding one tap away
pros: A new person sees things they can use straight away.
Programmers reach their section in one tap, and the app remembers.
cons: Programmers take one extra tap the first time.

options.label: Ask once on first open
pros: Everyone starts in the right place.
cons: A question before they have seen anything.

options.label: Keep it mixed
pros: Nothing is tucked away.
cons: Everyday listings stay outnumbered on every screen.

steps.path: Listings that are thin, unchecked or cannot be installed
steps.headline: Should browsing show only listings that meet a quality bar?
steps.today: Every listing is shown equally: ones with no description, ones never safety-checked, and 77 that cannot be installed at all.
steps.problem: You want the marketplace comprehensive, but thousands of thin listings bury the good ones. On 1 November you said things that cannot run should sit last with a note, not be hidden.
steps.proposal: A bar: safety-checked, described, has a preview, can be installed, and either picked by you or liked by real users. Pick how the bar is used.

options.label: Browse the best, search everything
pros: What you scroll through is all worth installing.
Nothing is removed: search, filters and 'Show everything' reach every listing.
A listing earns its way in automatically as people use and like it.
cons: A good new listing with no users yet is only found by search until it is picked or earns votes.

options.label: Show all, best first
pros: Everything is in the list; weak ones just sink to the bottom.
cons: Scrolling eventually reaches thousands of thin listings.

steps.path: The top of the screen: the big banner and the rows under it
steps.headline: Who should choose what appears in the top spots?
steps.today: You choose all of it by hand in one file, last changed in April. The first banner slot is wrong and nine featured items show 'Not checked'. There is no 'popular' or 'new' row because nothing is ranked.
steps.problem: On 28 August you asked how this could maintain itself. A hand list goes stale the week you get busy.

options.label: Automatic rows plus your picks
options.summary: Popular this week, New and rising, Top in each topic and 'Because you have X' fill themselves. Your picks sit beside them and each expires after a set time.
pros: The screen stays fresh without you touching it.
Your taste still leads the top of the page.
An old or broken pick drops out and is flagged to you rather than sitting there wrong.
cons: Automatic rows can surface something you would not have chosen.
Your picks need refreshing now and then, or that row empties.

options.label: Your picks only
pros: Full control of every slot.
cons: Goes stale exactly as it has since April.

options.label: Automatic only
pros: No upkeep at all.
cons: No personal voice; a new gem with few users never gets a push.

steps.page: How people feel, and how safe it is
steps.intro: What the marketplace knows about each listing, and what it tells people.

steps.path: What the app reports about installed listings
steps.headline: How much should the app count, so that 'popular' and 'working' mean something?
steps.today: The only number is how many signed-in people ever installed something. Removals are not counted, nor whether an update failed, nor whether anyone still uses it. Without sign-in the app reports nothing, and the privacy page promises that.
steps.problem: A ranking built on that is thin and easy to fake, and nobody finds out when an update breaks a plugin for everyone.
steps.proposal: The new counts are per listing only: installed, removed, update failed, used this week. Never what you typed or made. Pick who is counted.

options.label: Everyone, without names
options.summary: Each app sends plain counts tied to no account, with a switch in Settings to turn it off.
pros: Numbers are large enough to trust and hard to fake.
A broken update is caught within hours and paused.
cons: The privacy page changes: the app would report something without sign-in.
Some people will dislike any reporting, even nameless and switchable.

options.label: Signed-in people only
options.summary: Today's promise stays word for word.
pros: No change to the privacy promise.
cons: Small numbers: rankings wobble and broken updates are caught slowly.

options.label: No new counting
pros: Nothing new leaves anyone's computer.
cons: No 'popular', no health warnings, no automatic pause on a bad update.

steps.path: An update that can do more than the version you approved
steps.headline: If an update gives a plugin a new ability, should it ask you first?
steps.today: A listing's page lists what it can do, such as 'Runs commands on your computer'. An update can add to that list and nothing tells you.
steps.problem: A harmless plugin can become one that runs programs or reaches your accounts, in an update you pressed without looking.
steps.proposal: Yes: the Update button names the new ability and asks before applying it. 'Update all' skips those and lists them for you. No: updates stay one press and the new ability only shows on the page.

steps.path: The safety badge on each listing
steps.headline: Should the safety badge become a ladder that says exactly how far each listing was checked?
steps.today: The badge says 'Likely safe', 'Caution' or 'Not checked'. 'Likely safe' means an automatic scan found none of four known danger signs. No AI or person reads the plugin.
steps.problem: On 23 September you wanted to keep 'Likely safe' and make the check earn it. This morning you chose to reword it now. A ladder does both: each word means one exact thing, and the stronger words arrive as stronger checks are built.
steps.proposal: Four steps: Not checked · Checked (automatic scan) · Reviewed (an AI read this version) · Verified by YouCoded (a person did, or we made it). Caution overrides all of them.

options.label: Use the ladder
pros: Nobody is promised more than was done.
The AI review you asked for has an obvious place to show up.
Tapping the badge opens 'What we checked'.
cons: 'Checked' sounds less reassuring than 'Likely safe' until the AI review exists.

options.label: Keep 'Likely safe'
pros: No change to how listings look.
cons: The badge keeps overstating what the scan does.

steps.path: What makes an update reach people
steps.headline: Any change an author publishes reaches users as an update once it passes our checks.
steps.changed: The publishing guide tells authors an update reaches people only when they raise the version number. This morning's answer (updates follow the author's newest checked files) replaces that; the guide changes to match.
steps.notice: Updates stop getting stuck when an author forgets the number. The cost: a tiny change, such as a typo fix, also shows as an update.

steps.intro: The design covers all of it. This only sets the order.

steps.headline: After updates and installs are made reliable, what should come first?
steps.today: The first block is fixed: reliable installs and updates, then one shared list for every kind of thing. Everything else is built on those two.
steps.problem: The rest is several months of work. Its order decides what you and users feel soonest.

options.label: Finding and top spots
options.summary: Topics, Everyday/Coding, ranked search, automatic rows. Then safety, then Pages and new kinds.
pros: The marketplace looks and feels different soonest.
Needs no new reporting to start; the ranking sharpens later when counts arrive.
cons: Sharing Pages waits longest.

options.label: Safety and reporting
options.summary: The ladder, asking on new abilities, reports, the review queue, the AI review.
pros: The store is trustworthy before more people and more kinds arrive.
cons: Mostly invisible until something goes wrong.

options.label: Pages and new kinds
options.summary: Sharing Pages, publishing from the app, specialists, prompts, connected accounts.
pros: The newest, most distinctive part of the vision arrives first.
cons: More kinds pour into a store that still cannot rank or review them well.
Depends on the unfinished Pages work landing first.
